tier_rationale: The FCC grant for the parent/camera pair covers only 2410-2477 MHz under Part 15.247 as a spread-spectrum (FHSS) point-to-point transmitter, not an 802.11 Wi-Fi module (tagged proprietary_24ghz), and the vendor operates no cloud service for the product at all — there is no app, no account, and no remote-viewing feature to be optional. The camera and 5-inch parent monitor talk directly to each other on a closed link the owner holds both ends of.
the_unplug_test: Nothing changes, because there is nothing to unplug from. The camera and the handheld parent monitor form a direct 2.4 GHz link to each other, not to your router — there is no home Wi-Fi pairing step at all. You get local video and two-way talk on the 5-inch screen with a claimed range up to 1,000 feet. What you permanently do not get, with or without internet, is viewing from outside the house: this model has no app and no remote access, which some buyers consider the whole point and others consider the dealbreaker.

repairability.notes: Infant Optics sells standalone replacement cameras and parent units separately, which extends the life of a kit when one half fails or is lost.

sources.supports: FCC grant for the DXR-8 PRO (grantee Standard Merit Industrial Limited) covers 2410-2477 MHz as a Part 15 spread-spectrum transmitter only — no separate Wi-Fi or Bluetooth module appears in the filing, and the frequency plan is a proprietary FHSS video link rather than the 2.4 GHz band used for 802.11 Wi-Fi.

Independent review confirming the monitor uses a closed-loop '2nd Gen FHAA 2.4GHz' local wireless link with no app and no phone-based remote viewing — the reviewer names this the product's main drawback, which corroborates that there is no vendor cloud or companion app of any kind.
Current US retail listing at $199.99, used only for the price band, not for tier evidence.

open_questions: Confirm from the printed manual (fccid.io hosts it but blocked automated extraction) whether firmware is field-updatable at all; if there is no update mechanism, that is worth stating explicitly.
notes: The natural counterpoint to a Wi-Fi video monitor in this same subcategory: this one physically cannot be reached from outside the house because it never joins your network in the first place. The tradeoff is real — no remote viewing, ever, by design — and some parents will prefer a Wi-Fi model for that reason. This record makes no claim about which is better, only what each one requires.
